title: Word Search & Grid Backtracking
summary: DFS-with-backtracking over a 2D grid to match a path against a target word, including the mark-and-restore pattern that makes 'unexplore' work on a grid.

slides.markdown:
Word Search asks: does a path of adjacent cells (up/down/left/right, no cell reused) spell out a target word? It's the [backtracking framework](backtracking-framework) applied to a grid instead of an array — the grid is really just a graph where every cell's neighbors are its four (or fewer, at the edges) adjacent cells, and the search is a DFS that backtracks the instant a step stops matching.

The one genuinely new idea versus array-based backtracking: **"unexplore" on a grid usually means mutating the grid in place** (marking a cell visited, then restoring it) rather than maintaining a separate structure — a pattern that shows up in almost every grid-search interview problem, not just this one.

slides.sectionTitle: The grid as a graph of neighbors
slides.markdown:
Treat every cell `(r, c)` as a graph node whose neighbors are `(r-1,c)`, `(r+1,c)`, `(r,c-1)`, `(r,c+1)` — whichever of those four fall inside the grid's bounds. Matching the target word becomes DFS from a candidate starting cell: if the current cell's letter matches the word's current character, recurse into each neighbor to match the next character; if it doesn't match, this path is dead and backtracks immediately.

The base case is matching the full word length — reaching that means every character along the path matched, and the search can return success without looking at any more neighbors. There's no separate "choose/explore/unexplore" vocabulary needed beyond what backtracking-framework already established; a grid is simply a graph with a very regular, predictable neighbor structure.

slides.sectionTitle: Mark and restore — the grid's unexplore step
In-place marking vs. a separate visited set
slides.markdown:
An alternative to mutating the board is keeping a separate `visited` set of `(r, c)` coordinates, checked and updated instead of overwriting the cell. It's correct, but it costs real, avoidable extra memory: O(word length) auxiliary space for the set on top of the recursion's own stack depth, versus **zero** extra space for in-place marking since the mutation reuses memory the board already occupies.

The in-place trick specifically works because the sentinel value ('#', or any character guaranteed not to appear in the alphabet the word is drawn from) can never accidentally match a real letter — so a later step in the same path can't walk back onto a cell already committed to the current path and mistake it for an unvisited one. When that guarantee doesn't hold (say, the sentinel could collide with real data), a visited set becomes the safer, if costlier, choice.

slides.sectionTitle: Pruning the instant a character mismatches
slides.markdown:
The `board[r][c] != word[i]` check inside `dfs` is the entire pruning mechanism — a branch dies the moment the current cell's letter doesn't match the word's current position, before any further recursion into that cell's neighbors happens at all. There's no need for a separate "is this branch still viable" pass; the character comparison itself is the validity check, evaluated fresh at every single cell visited.

This is what keeps the search from degenerating into exploring every possible path in the grid — for a word of length L, the vast majority of starting cells and directions fail the character check within the first step or two, long before reaching anywhere near length L.

slides.sectionTitle: The search tree from one starting cell
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a small grid (4x4) with a target word overlaid as a search tree rooted at one starting cell — the tree shows up to 4 branches per node (one per direction), most branches drawn crossed-out/pruned at the exact depth where the cell's letter first fails to match the next character of the word, and one surviving path drawn solid all the way to a leaf marked "word found" >>>

Most branches die within one or two levels — the tree is wide (branching factor up to 4) but shallow in practice for any given failed direction, since a mismatch is detected immediately rather than after building out a longer path.

slides.sectionTitle: Trying every cell as a start point
slides.markdown:
The word's first letter could appear anywhere in the grid, so the outer loop tries **every** cell as a candidate starting point, running a full DFS from each one. This is why the overall complexity is dominated by the number of cells, not just the search from a single start: with `rows × cols` starting points and up to 4 directions explored at each of up to `word length` steps, the worst case is roughly **O(rows × cols × 4^L)** for a word of length L.

In practice this is far better than the worst case suggests, because most starting cells fail on the very first character comparison (the letter simply doesn't match), so the `4^L` factor is only paid by the small fraction of starting cells whose first letter actually matches the word.

slides.sectionTitle: One word vs. many words at once
slides.markdown:
| | Searching for one word | Searching for many words at once |
|---|---|---|
| Data structure | The word itself, compared character by character | A **trie** built from all target words, shared across the whole grid search |
| Pruning | Character mismatch at the current position | Trie has no child for the current character — the *shared prefix* fails, ruling out every word sharing that prefix in one check |
| Redundant work | None — one search per word if run separately | Massive if run per-word — a shared prefix like "CAR" gets re-walked once per word starting with it, unless a trie unifies them |
| Complexity | O(rows × cols × 4^L) for one word of length L | Roughly the same per starting cell, but shared across all words simultaneously — one grid pass finds every match |

Running the single-word search once per word in a list re-explores the same dead ends over and over, once per word that happens to share a prefix. A trie collapses all of them into one pass: at each DFS step, only cells whose letter has a matching child in the trie are worth recursing into at all, which prunes far more aggressively than a plain character comparison ever could.

```python
# BUG: checks the character before confirming the coordinates are in bounds
def dfs(r, c, i):
    if board[r][c] != word[i]:   # IndexError if r or c is out of range
        return False
    ...
```

The bounds check `0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols` must run **before** indexing into `board[r][c]`, not after — Python (and most languages) doesn't short-circuit an out-of-range index just because a later check would have caught it; it raises immediately. This surfaces the moment a search reaches an edge or corner cell and tries a direction that walks off the grid, which happens on nearly every real input, not just adversarial ones — so it's a bug that shows up fast in testing, but only if the edges are actually exercised.

slides.sectionTitle: Why long words prune fast in practice
slides.markdown:
The worst-case bound O(rows × cols × 4^L) looks terrifying for long words, but longer words are actually **easier** in practice, not harder: every additional character is one more chance for the path to mismatch and die early. A 15-letter word needs 15 consecutive correct matches just to survive to the base case — vanishingly unlikely on a random grid — so almost every branch is pruned within the first few characters regardless of how long the target word is.

The genuinely hard case for this algorithm is a **short** word on a grid with lots of repeated letters (say, a 3-letter word on a grid that's mostly one repeated character) — that's when the branching factor of 4 actually gets to compound close to its full worst-case depth, because matches keep surviving instead of dying immediately.
